:::{#rem-choosing-k}
#### Choosing the number of folds

The number of folds $\nfolds$ trades bias against variance
in the cross-validation estimate itself
[@james2021islr2e, sec. 5.1.4]:

- **Bias.**
  Each [fitted model](#def-fitted-model) in @eq-cv-estimate is fitted to about $\nobs (\nfolds - 1) / \nfolds$ observations.
  A model fitted to fewer observations usually has a larger [generalization error](#def-generalization-error),
  so $\cvest{\nfolds}$ tends to overstate the [expected generalization error](#def-expected-generalization-error) of a model fitted to all $\nobs$.
  The overstatement shrinks as $\nfolds$ grows.
- **Variance.**
  As $\nfolds$ grows,
  the $\nfolds$ training sets overlap more,
  so the $\nfolds$ [fitted models](#def-fitted-model) are more alike
  and their errors may be more strongly correlated.
  An average of strongly correlated errors varies more
  from one data set to another than an average of weakly correlated ones.
  This is a heuristic, not a theorem [@hastie2009elements, sec. 7.10].
  How correlated the errors are depends on how much the fitted model changes
  when one observation changes,
  so for a stable fitting method the variance need not rise with $\nfolds$.
- **Computation.**
  The model is fitted $\nfolds$ times.

$\nfolds = 5$ or $\nfolds = 10$ is the usual compromise.

:::
